speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I address my question to the acting secretary of state: it concerns the situation in Angola, the overnight developments. While the reports of the operation differ, there seems to be little doubt now that South African troops did cross the border into Angola. Would the minister, first of all, clarify the nature of this operation? Also, in light of the strong criticism which the United States has levelled against South Africa, can the minister say what the Canadian reaction is?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to add very much detail, except to tell the hon. member that we have asked our embassy in Capetown to tell the government of South Africa that Canada is deeply concerned about this military incursion into the territory of a neighbouring sovereign state. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will put my supplementary question to the right hon. Prime Minister. It seems to me there is a direct contradiction here in government policy. On one hand, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the government is phasing out, and will not have, any operations with South Africa of a commercial nature. Yesterday, in committee, the Minister of Finance said, "We do not put any restriction on the people who should participate in the extension of credit."
Is it the policy of the government to have one set of standards for the private sector, and another set of standards for the government in its dealings with South Africa?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRADE WITH SOUTH AFRICA-ALLEGED CONTRADICTION IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
No. Mr. Speaker, we do not want to have two sets of standards. I think the Minister of Finance is correct in saying that he will investigate this matter. I must say that as an uninformed amateur in what is being borrowed and the way it is being done, I cannot particularly see that a man who is going to borrow from somebody else and asks him to lend him money worries where that person is getting the money. This is in the nature, I would think, of a tertiary boycott: we are going to borrow from some people, then we are going to find out where they got the money from, who lent it to them, and so on.
It seems to me that in the nature of a commercial operation, you borrow money from a respectable lender and that should settle the matter, as far as I am concerned. However, I am

prepared to be informed further by the inquiry that the Minister of Finance says he is going to embark upon.

subtopic: TRADE WITH SOUTH AFRICA-ALLEGED CONTRADICTION IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect, I cannot follow that reasoning at all. Either the Government of Canada has a policy of not dealing in commercial transactions with South Africa, or it has not. The fact that the government is going out to borrow money would indicate to me that it has an obligation to make very clear whether it is dealing with South African commercial transactions or not. It seems to me that the fact the government needs the money should make no difference either way: we either have that policy, or we do not.
I ask if Citibank, the lead bank, is negotiating with South Africa or, to put it the other way, will the government instruct the lead bank in this standby credit not to deal with South African banks in the development of the resources?

I would be glad to hear from him, too; but for the moment I am speaking to his colleague on his left, through you, Mr. Speaker.
We are not borrowing from South Africa; we are borrowing from Citibank. Where Citibank gets the money is not an immediate problem to me. If it is to the hon. member, I would be interested in hearing argument. The Minister of Finance said he is going to look into that. I have risen in this House against the idea of tertiary boycotts. Maybe this is a case where the hon. member is suggesting this is the way we should proceed. We are borrowing from somebody who wants to lend to us. FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS COMPENSATION TO QUEBEC FOR LOSS OF SALES TAX REVENUE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister and concerns the Ottawa-Quebec conflict over the sales tax reimbursement.
As there is more and more agreement with the fact that Ottawa should respect the provincial jurisdiction over the sales tax and that it should therefore reimburse the province of Quebec the $186 million which is at the base of the present discussion which is going on through the media, is the right hon. Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance prepared to meet the premier or the minister of finance of Quebec to come to an agreement which would be in the spirit of the constitution, rather than trying to buy votes in Quebec by reimbursing each individual, as the latest rumours would have it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS COMPENSATION TO QUEBEC FOR LOSS OF SALES TAX REVENUE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member speaks of respecting the constitution and adds that the sales tax comes under provincial jurisdiction. We wholeheartedly agree. That is why the Minister of Finance went to all provincial finance ministers saying: You have this tax, would you be willing to cut it if we reimbursed you? Nine provinces said yes. We never said that this tax came under our jurisdiction. We offered the provinces money to do something. Nine said yes, the tenth one, Quebec, gave no reply.
We never maintained and we do not maintain now that we have the power to lower the sales tax in Quebec. We only said that if Quebec agreed to do certain things, like the other provinces, we would give it money. If it does not want to go along, we certainly will not interfere in its jurisdiction. We will arrange for this money to go to Quebeckers through some other means. The hon. member seems to object to the fact that this money would go to individual Quebeckers, I do not know why; perhaps he could indicate it in a supplementary question.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS COMPENSATION TO QUEBEC FOR LOSS OF SALES TAX REVENUE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary question.

In his reply, the Prime Minister stated that he does not interfere in the provincial administration or in the provincial jurisdiction, but by laying down to the provinces a condition which is explicitly rejected by Quebec he is compelling Quebec and the other provinces to meet the requirements of the federal government. This is the central issue of all current discussions and disputes between Quebec and the federal government. It is a bad approach for future discussions on a new Canadian constitution. Now I am concerned about the dangers of giving directly all those funds to Quebec and this is the question which the Prime Minister asked me-

We say: How would you go about it? Let us discuss the matter. And seven provinces agreed with the formula suggested by Mr. Chretien. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the following question will be answered today: 1,149.

1.	How many fatalities in Canada were related to exposure to winter cold in
(a)	1972 (b) 1973 (c) 1974 (d) 1975 (e) 1976?
2.	How many serious cases of frostbite were reported in Canada in (a) 1972
(b)	1973 (c) 1974 (d) 1975 (e) 1976?
3.	To which common illnesses in Canada can the winter cold be considered to be a significant contributing or complicating factor?
4.	What studies have been carried out by the government into the risks offered to the health of Canadians by styles of clothing affording adequate protection from winter cold?

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of National Health and Welfare and National Defence as follows: 1. According to Statistics Canada data, the numbers of deaths reported due to excessive cold (code E901, ICDA-8 revised) in these years were: (a) 1972, 111; (b) 1973, 122; (c) 1974, 123;
(d)	1975, 104. (e) Data for 1976 are not yet available.
2.	According to Statistics Canada data, the numbers of admissions to general and allied special hospitals in Canada for frostbite, excessive cold and freezing (codes 991.0, 991.1, 991.2, 991.3 and 991.9, ICDA-8 revised) in these years were: (a) 1972, 1,059; (b) 1973, 559; (c) 1974, 672; (d) 1975, 590;
(e)	1976,-Data for this year are not yet available.
3.	It is a common observation that an increase in the frequency of colds occurs in the winter. Sometimes this has been correlated with sharp changes in the temperature, humidity or pollution of the air, but the popular belief that cold weather causes common colds cannot be substantiated from epidemiologic observations in the arctic or tropics or from studies in volunteers. Exposure of volunteer subjects to cold did not activate latent respiratory viruses. The reason for the apparent relation between the season and common colds remains unclear. However, winter cold is recognized to be a contributing factor in the syndrome of hypothermia. This condition is not common in Canada. Winter cold is also a predisposing factor in a number of unrelated accidents and illnesses. For example: unusual exercise (shovelling snow) is responsible for precipitating numerous myocardial infarctions, and icy roads and sidewalks cause people to slip and fall, resulting in broken bones, strains and sprains.
4.	With respect to the National Health Research and Development Program, no projects have been funded relating to clothing affording adequate protection from winter cold. The Department of National Defence has carried out long term studies on the research, development, testing and evaluation of winter clothing systems designed to provide optimum protection for Canadian Forces personnel operating in the cold. DND also instructs and trains servicemen on the proper use and care of this equipment and related materiel to ensure that correct and safe cold weather procedures are employed to minimize risks and hazards to health which may result from exposure to winter cold.

Of course I am not suggesting by my remarks today that a finger should be pointed to the CNR particularly, but that there should be some system set up to strengthen the accountability of Crown corporations to parliament. We have many examples, and I do not want to stray too far from this particular legislation. But I am sure an exasperating feeling comes on a member of parliament when he starts to ask questions about Crown corporations.
I remember asking a question once about the CBC. I had heard a rumour-my questions are only sometimes based on rumours-but I will put it this way that I had heard a story that the CBC had spent considerable amounts of money for the creation of a new logo. As a parliamentarian, due to inquiries I had received from constituents about this expenditure, I felt it was my duty to inquire into how much was spent for the production of this new logo for the CBC. In response to a question on the order paper I was told that it was not in the interests of the corporation to give this information to parliamentarians, let alone to the public, that somehow this was a matter of internal financial management and concern, and therefore was not available to me as a member of parliament. Commercial considerations notwithstanding, that kind of approach is all too prevalent with respect to questions relating to financial operations of Crown corporations.
If we are to create these Crown corporations and have them go into public markets and into business of one sort or another, and if we are expected to fund and pay for these Crown corporations, the very minimum we should expect is to have some reasonable ability through parliament to examine and scrutinize the legitimacy of expenditures and the advisability of spending, not just in the past, but also in the future.
The committee, in this particular instance, dealt in an unfortunate way with the suggestions that I made about strengthening the accountability of the CNR. The committee, dominated as it is by government members, used the flimsy excuse that this request was an attempt to stall passage of the bill. As a result it refused to allow the Auditor General or a
Railway Act
representative from his office to appear before the committee respecting suggestions that might be coming from that office relating to the examination of expenditures, policies, and procedures within the CNR.
I want to deal at this point with the CNR in terms of rail transportation and in particular with an aspect of vital interest to me and, I am sure, to all members from western Canada. This concerns a theme I have been bringing forward in parliament from time to time with the government and particularly with the Minister of Transport, without much success, I am sorry to say. This relates to the effect of the recommendations of the Hall commission. In my view, in the terms of the efficiency of the operation of the CNR, and indeed the operation of the other railway system in Canada, and the implications as far as western Canada and the Hall commission are concerned, these recommendations are of the utmost importance. As parliamentarians representing not only the interests of western Canada but looking at the situation in the national context we should be most interested in and supportive of these recommendations.
What brings me to talk about the Hall commission as it relates to the CNR and the other railway is the attitude which the minister has been taking regarding the recommendations of the Hall commission. Reluctant is maybe too soft a term to use about the attitude which I have detected coming from the Minister of Transport concerning the total package of the Hall commission.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I asked a question of the minister with respect to the proposal in the report of the Hall commission concerning the extension of the Crowsnest rates relating to livestock, meat, and finished products. I received a negative answer. The gist of the minister's answer was that this would somehow involve an enormous amount of money. He could not see his way clear, I suppose, to recommend to his colleagues in cabinet that the amount of money required to put into effect the recommendations set out in the Hall commission report would be legitimate expenditures for western Canada. I was sorry to hear that negative response from the minister, coming as he does from western Canada.
I get the impression more and more that the minister in his own mind thinks these proposals will mean a large amount of money, which he indicates, but he does not specify what the amount is. He talks about vast amounts of money. The fact of the matter is, in my opinion, that the amount of money involved is not in the first place an increase in the expenditure that we are now facing respecting transportation facilities in western Canada as it relates to rail, but indeed they are nominal expenditures to place western Canada more in a position of equity concerning freight rates paid on the products to which I have referred.
I do not think there is any question the railways should be adequately and properly compensated for the goods which they carry, as a general principle. However, if one examines the record and looks over the past financial statements of the railway, the years in which the profits were greatest were the years in which the railway carried a large tonnage of grain.

That is a very important comparison. When the railways carried a lot of grain, that was the time when profits were the highest. Somehow I think the people in Canada believe that the moneys expended through Crowsnest and other methods are being poured into western Canada particularly as some sort of unrecoverable subsidy. Nothing could be farther from the truth.
The expenditure for transportation of grain is an expenditure and investment by the people of Canada in their own interest. I made this point in the last debate we had on transportation policy on the last allotted day. It concerned the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). I tried to demonstrate that payments which are being made for the delivery of grain, and payments with respect to grain generally, in the final analysis accrue to the benefit of people in central Canada. This relates to the cost of bread as well as in other ways in which the western farmer, out of his own pocket, subsidizes the consumer in central Canada. That should be understood. The fact is the government has a very peculiar concept of the way in which subsidies with regard to grain delivery ought to be handled.
When I first came to this House I was confronted with a speech made by the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, in Edmonton. At that time he cast some doubt on this government's determination to retain the statutory Crownsnest Pass rates within Canada. That caused me the greatest of concern. Since that time the minister has wriggled and wriggled to avoid coming down and getting away from the original statement. However, there is still suspicion in the mind of every western Canadian as to his dedication to the retention of the statutory Crowsnest Pass rates.
By subsequent statements the minister has merely exacerbated that concern in western Canada. Although he has not yet articulated it fully, it appears he has some idea of changing the whole basis of payment of any compensation to western Canadians. Rather than the proposition of payments to the railways for the short haul, payments will be made directly by cheque, I take it signed by the minister, to farmers across western Canada, on a cultivated acreage basis. The minister has the idea of individualizing these payments. While that proposition may be politically attractive in the mind of the minister, it is a waste of the taxpayers' money. It is an inefficient and wrong attitude to take toward the payment of the subsidy.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
My colleague says "shades of Jimmy Gardiner." One reason people in western Canada are so adamant about retaining the statutory Crowsnest Pass rates is that it takes away any sense of arbitrariness, either on the part of this government or the Conservatives when they form the government after the next election, with regard to the basis upon which payments will be made with respect to Crowsnest.
There is a built-in advantage now with Crowsnest as far as international trade is concerned. It helps us remain competi-

tive in the sale of grain. It assists in maintaining some reasonable balance of trade. However, once it is left at the discretion of any government, whether Liberal or Conservative, an arbitrary aspect comes into the matter. This makes western Canadians very nervous. It should be left in the statute. In that way, any changes are made by act of parliament and public discussion, not by order in council or some order taken by cabinet in the dead of night without the fullest discussion and public participation.
From what I can gather, the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board feels that the farmer should pay the full shot, that is to say, the compensatory rate for carrying grain, and the difference between the Crow rates and the compensatory rates would be paid to the farmer by the government. I suggest that on this basis the farmer would be without the use of his money for a period of 12 to 18 months. This is another suggestion put forward by the minister.
I want to deal with another aspect before terminating my remarks, that is, the concept of extending the Crowsnest Pass rates which I raised in the House yesterday. The Hall commission recommended that rates on livestock and meat products be set at levels which do not discriminate against the national locational advantage of prairie livestock producers and processors. Presently the compensatory level of rates on meat and meat products and the low statutory level of grain rates distort the locational advantage.
The Hall commission further recommended that the present statutory levels of grain rates remain in force. Therefore, a subsidy would be required to remove the current rate distortion on livestock and meat products. What does this amount to?
The Hall commission recommendations must be construed to mean that livestock and meat rates are to be "Crow related" or subsidized to the extent of grain consumed by the animal unit concerned. The often stated belief that the Hall Commission advocated the extension of Crow rates to livestock and meat is just not correct.
In the case of beef, a 1,050 pound live steer will have consumed 4,120 pounds of barley to reach that marketable weight. If you look at Volume I of that report, table 9-6 at page 306, that is the basis of the contention and point that I am now making.
Second, a 1,050 pound live steer will dress out at 550 pounds of beef as meat and meat products. Assuming that the costs of moving grain are 2.6 times the Crow rate, the movement of grain is subsidized to the extent of 35 cents per 100 pounds. The Crow subsidy of 35.2 cents per hundredweight equals $14.50 per steer. This is based on the assumption that a steer consumes 4,120 pounds of barley times 35.2. That would equal $14.50.
The $14.50 per steer subsidy equals $1.38 per one hundred pounds subsidy on live cattle, or $2.63 per hundred pounds on dressed meat and meat products. In 1974, the last year the commission had before it, the movement of live beef from west to east totalled 160,000 tons, and the movement of meat and
May 5, 1978

meat products totalled 157,000 tons. This is verified at page 294 of the report. The subsidy "Crow related" rates on beef and meat products totals, live beef 160,000 tons times (1.38 x 20), $4,416,000, and dressed beef 157,000 tons times (2.63 x 20), $8,258,200, for a total of $12,674,200.
I now move on to deal with hogs. I want to document this because I know the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board will read this speech very carefully. I do not think he understands the recommendations of the Hall commission. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) is often in the House. I know he listens. He will pass on the basis of my remarks to the minister and aid him in understanding the recommendations of the Hall commission.
Notwithstanding this very important report, the minister unfortunately has not taken upon himself to see its author and architect in order to get an explanation so that he can fully understand what is going on as far as the report is concerned. A 200-pound live hog consumes 600 pounds of barley and dresses out at 160 pounds of pork products. In 1975, the flow of pork west to east equalled 6.5 per cent of Canadian production of 7.5 million head, or 490,000 head. A Crow subsidy of 35.2 per hundredweight on grain would be the equivalent of $2.11 per head of hogs on the basis of their consuming 600 pounds of barley. The total subsidy necessary to equalize hog rates to Crow grain rates totals $1,033,900 per year.
I put forward these statistics to show that any increase in livestock production as a result of equalization of rates through the extension of the Crow subsidy to livestock would not result in an increase in total subsidy expenditures, since the difference would be made up from increased grain shipments. This is a point which seems to have escaped the minister.
In his answers to questions put to him from this side of the House the minister shrugs off suggestions we make to improve the transportation system in western Canada. He tells us the government is already making large sums available for transportation and that, in a period of restraint, it is not possible to consider further large expenditures. However, he knows that the effect of rail line abandonment as recommended by the commission-I believe some 2,160 miles of branch line are involved-will be a saving to the federal treasury of roughly $400 million annually.
What happens when we come forward and ask that maybe $30 million extra a year be considered with respect to extending the Crow rate in such a way as to help the livestock producers of western Canada? The minister says he cannot afford the money. How can the minister justify this parsimonious attitude? Does he not have sufficient influence in cabinet to persuade his colleagues to accept the reasonable proposition I have put forward? The minister always puts his case in terms of spending money in western Canada, though he must realize that we in western Canada are losing money which has been forthcoming directly or indirectly through the subsidy program.

That would be required to give western Canadians a small indication that Ottawa understands and is sympathetic to the hopes and aspirations of western Canada and our desire to take advantage of our location as the breadbasket of the world and the centre of the livestock industry in Canada.
The minister's attitude mystifies me. After all, only a week or so ago we were asked to agree to extend the scope of the EDC to $25 billion. Here is a request from western Canadians for an expenditure of something like $30 million. If it were accepted, the gesture would go a long way to making westerners feel that there is at least some concern being shown by the federal government about the way in which rates have been treated in the past, and some desire to encourage farmers and processors. It is not asking for the world, by any means, especially in the light of the savings which will be made by the closing down of branch lines and the cutting off of certain subsidies.
It is not hard to see where the government's priorities lie. Its interest is, as ever, political: win the two central provinces and forget the hinterland. That is what the government thinks and talks about.
My hon. friend from Carleton-Charlotte was misquoted by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). He is a spokesman for the interests of Atlantic Canada and the maritime provinces, and he expressed a natural concern about the situation there. What he said was not that western Canada was getting all the attention but that eastern Canada was getting no attention with respect to its serious transportation problems. He got up on a question of privilege to correct the record, and I can understand his exasperation. The government is concerned only with keeping its power base, regardless of the consequences for western Canada and the maritimes. The hinterlands are a low priority when it comes to transportation policy.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am encouraged that you are stopping the squealing from the other side, and I know you are as repulsed as I am by the interjections. As far as transportation policy is concerned, we on this side are interested and extend our congratulations to the president of the CNR. As I say, he has taken hold of this Crown corporation, and I congratulate him on the admirable job he has done. I have no quarrel with Mr. Bandeen. Every once in a while I write to him about a particular grievance I have.
We all know in western Canada that CN transport is "out" as far as Saskatchewan is concerned. Many of the towns in my constituency have suffered a loss of services. It is my duty, as it is the duty of every member representing a Saskatchewan constituency, to attempt to resist what we consider to be a short term and misguided policy. But as to the operation of the railway there seems to be a new sense of enthusiasm and optimism. I repeat that I do not take issue with management in a serious way. I do object to the attitude of the government with respect to transportation and the constraints within which the government places the operations of our railways.
I want to allude just briefly to another grievance we in western Canada have about the way in which rail passenger service is developing. I realize that support for rail passenger policy is sometimes based upon a rather romantic view many of us have with respect to railways, but for a long time we have heard the argument that rail passenger service is on the way out. I am concerned that rail passenger service is not being given a serious chance. I hope that VIA Rail will do something to change my mind in that regard.
As we look at what is happening to trans-continental rail passenger service, there is nothing but apprehension and concern on the part of western Canadians. My colleague, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), has pointed out some of the ludicrous scheduling propositions which are being laid down for transcontinental passenger service. It is not the kind of scheduling which will encourage people to travel on trains.
I took my family on a train east from Saskatoon last summer when we had a chance to take a little holiday. It was a superb trip. The service was excellent. There was a fine staff and fine food. I do not think we are doing enough to encourage patronage at this very crucial time, in view of energy consumption forecasts and energy costs, to retain the basis of our rail passenger service, especially in terms of trans-Canada service and passenger service. I support policies which encourage continuation and expansion of fast, efficient, and enjoyable rail passenger service. I think that point of view is shared by members of my party generally.
I have indicated my concern about accountability of Crown corporations and the necessity of having a serious look at that, especially in terms of legislation such as this which deals with refinancing the CNR. We had an excellent opportunity to

have the Auditor General come before the committee to give us his views on the expenditures and the control of expenditures within the corporation, but the government backed away from that on very flimsy grounds.
As pointed out by my colleagues, this bill should have been deferred until the Royal Commission on Government Management handed down its recommendations, or at least until the government produced the legislation promised by the Minister of Transport for the next session regarding Crown corporations.
In my opinion this bill is premature. I do not want to speak much longer, but I want to express as strongly as I am able to do some of my concerns and some of the concerns which have been expressed to me by western Canadians generally with respect to the direction in which transportation policy in this country has taken us. The most important aspect of that in western Canada relates to rail transportation.
I want to leave with the House and with the minister some of the concerns of hon. members on his side of the House with respect to the way in which this government and the Minister of Transport have failed to deal with the key recommendations of the Hall commission. As I said before, it is our view that the chief commissioner, the Hon. Emmett Hall, should be consulted. He is the architect and chief spokesman of the Hall commission, and his expertise with respect to the implementation of the recommendations contained in his report ought to be used. If the government persists in refusing to do this, we can only assume that it has no interest in putting into effect the key recommendations of the commission. The Prairie Rail Action Committee was set up by the minister rather than by the prairie rail authority which was recommended by the Hall commission.
There is every appearance of a stall, and this will put us right back to where we were before the commission handed down its recommendations. We are going to be under the control of the eastern-dominated Canadian Transport Commission. The people of western Canada are concerned that they will not have enough input as far as transportation policy is concerned in western Canada. They do not feel that they are getting a fair hearing. 1 am simply reporting that the people of western Canada do not feel a sense of participation in the development of transportation policy in western Canada. There is an opportunity to have consultation on the Hall commission recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part in the third reading debate on this bill in order to refer to some ramifications, such as further public and private action in respect of transportation, particularly rail transportation in this country, and I hope this action will be taken with some measure of urgency.
At the outset let me say that in our caucus we approved of the passage of this legislation. We have been asking in this party for recapitalization of the CNR both long before and ever since I came to this House in 1968. In fact, sir, we could make some arguments in favour of greater recapitalization than is proposed in this bill.
I have difficulty understanding the reasoning of the official opposition in moving a six months hoist. We spent many days on this bill, and colleagues in the Conservative party seized many opportunities to go into detailed questioning of the management of Canadian National, of the minister, and other witnesses. Members of the committee obtained the passage of one amendment to the bill which was approved of by members on all sides. We obtained the passage of another amendment yesterday at the report stage. All members agreed to that, but now members of that party want to hoist the bill for six months. I had thought they might now be happier with the bill and that, other than a few hours of debate at third reading, we could proceed to let it pass. In spite of that inconsistency on their part, I hope this legislation receives approval over the next few sitting days so that we can get on with the job that needs to be done in this country, particularly in respect of rail transportation.
If the passage of this legislation makes it easier for the CNR to do a better job in respect of its cash flow and in terms of capital expenditures for the needed improvements to the system, then it seems to me this is a worth-while bill. It seems to me also that additional public investment and direction by this parliament and the Ministry of Transport are required both in respect of the investment of monies and the priorities on the part of the railroads regarding improvements to be made to the system over the next five or six years.
There is also a need for a change of heart on the part of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in terms of the activities of that group in the prairie provinces which is in some respects subverting and perverting the recommendations of the Hall commission. I refer to the Prairie Rail Action Committee which should at this point be disbanded. The minister should ask for the resignations of its members. In fact I would even suggest a reconstitution of the Hall commission to carry out the decision-making over the next year or two regarding the two thousand and more miles of track to be considered for improvement and inclusion in the basic rail network.
This PRAC group has made three recommendations recently that I suggest are horrendous. They fly in the face of the

demands of the people in the areas affected; they fly in the face of the wishes of the railway companies as well as the elevator companies, and are contrary to the submissions to the commission and the recommendations of the Hall commission itself.
Surely when the Prairie Rail Action Committee makes recommendations concerning certain branch lines or parts of branch lines, which fly in the face of all these things, the Minister of Transport should make a journey out west to sit down with these boys and have a heart to heart talk, or get their resignations. I wish to mention specifically four items which are under the purview of this so-called Prairie Rail Action Committee-it is more of a destruction committee. The committee has recommended that the line from Shamrock to Courval be abandoned, in spite of and in the face of what the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool says, that is, that there are three primary elevator points on that line which they intend to upgrade or build new facilities. That is in the constituency of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), and I sus-ect the Minister of Transport will be hearing further repres itations on that.
Another one is in my own area, the Colonsay subdivision where, in spite of the fact the Hall commission recommends that the entire line is a heavy grain line and, to quote the Hall commission, must be maintained, the minister's committee

recommends that the south end of the line from Liberty to Dilke be abandoned. That line moves 60,000 bushels per mile per year, and there are a couple of viable communities there, particularly Holdfast. I feel sorry for the poor Liberal candidate who runs around in that area. They will run him out of town, tarred and feathered, and send him back to the Minister of Transport.
Another line that is even more serious runs from Eston to Lacadena. That line moves 90,000 bushels of grain per mile of track and CNR wants to keep it, but the minister's committee recommends that it be abandoned. We do not need that kind of help in western Canada.
Members of the commission told me-I have already mentioned this on another occasion in the House, but I will remind the minister of it-that in the case of the Colonsay subdivision, for example, their reasoning for recommending that it be put under the proposed prairie rail authority was so that it would receive first priority for rehabilitation, rebuilding, and returning it to the basic rail network in western Canada. That was their reason; otherwise they would have put it in the basic network in the first place.

As I recall the Hall recommendations they did not say that, but said in actual words that it was too soon to judge whether some lines should be kept. The members of that commission made it very plain at a meeting of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool or the National Farmers' Union, and it does not matter which, when I questioned them personally, that this was the case in respect of the Colonsay subdivision, which I specifically mentioned. I understand that in the case of many other subdivisions their reasoning for recommending they be under a prairie rail authority was in order that they receive priority.
The minister shakes his head, but I could call many witnesses to retell him what they heard when the commission was questioned about that particular subdivision and about other lines. It was my understanding, and I may have been wrong, that the basic rail network would be a major responsibility of the railways themselves, because they are their most lucrative lines in the main. Those are the secondary main lines and the most heavily used branch lines on which the railways do not
May 5, 1978

lose any money, or, if they do, lose very little. I just do not understand the priority the minister places on helping the railways to upgrade the lines in the basic network before looking after the ones in the network that need to be upgraded and added to the basic system.
There is another subdivision about which many people are waiting to hear what the Prairie Rail Action Committee has to say. I hope the minister will tell that committee ahead of time that it better not play around with that line which runs from Sturgis to Kelvington through Preeceville. That one had better be upgraded and put into the basic network very quickly. Kelvington is a community of over 1,000 people and Preeceville is a community of over 1,100 people; there are over 12 delivery points on that line with a ten year average of 8.3 million bushels of grain; 73,000 bushels per mile of line. We need a decision, and we need it quickly, for that line to be upgraded, rehabilitated, and placed in the basic rail network, and we do not need any playing around by the tame committee the minister appointed, in my opinion, to give the railways everything they asked for in the first place before the Hall commission was appointed.
Let me move to another area where there needs to be urgent and immediate action involving investment and capital allocation. Whether we recapitalize the CNR to the extent this bill allows, the direction of future capital investment, the direction of the investment of the Canadian Pacific and additional public investment voted by the Parliament of Canada, as well as drawing upon private investment to the tune of several billions of dollars, are a necessity in respect of transportation in this country.
Let me illustrate what I mean. In the area of electrification of rail lines in Canada-North America for that matter-we are lagging far behind other countries. More important, we are wasting energy and wasting an opportunity to move quickly. To do the right thing in the way of operating our rail system in this country would create employment and would be a remarkable investment in the assets of this nation in respect of rail transportation.
The Syncrude project is to cost about $3 billion. To electrify 5,000 miles of rail line in western Canada would cost in the order of $1 billion, including the cost of purchasing electric locomotives. The electrification of 1,000 miles of track a year over the next fives years would mean a total saving in crude oil equivalent of 43 million barrels. In terms of energy value, allowing about $1 billion per year for the electricity required, the savings would be some $400 million a year. With the price of oil being $11, $12 or $13 a barrel, the savings would be far more than enough to complete the entire electrification of the railway system.
I want to tell this House, and I know the minister and the people in his department already know this, that the saving of about 33 million barrels of oil per year, or a total of 43 million barrels of crude oil equivalent, is almost exactly the same as the output of the Syncrude development which is to cost about $3 billion. In other words, the electrification of 5,000 miles of railway track in western Canada would save more oil at a cost
Railway Act
of $1 billion than Syncrude will produce at a cost of $3 billion. What kind of capital investment direction is that?
I suggest the government has gone at this backwards. We could electrify 9,000 miles of railway lines in Canada, including the cost of purchasing the electric locomotives, at a savings of crude oil equivalent equal to the amount of energy equivalent used by Air Canada each year, and at a cost lower than the cost of operations in the tar sands of Alberta. We have to develop the tar sands in Alberta, but it seems to me we have placed the priorities in the wrong order. Other countries have moved into electrification at a rate which we should be moving.
When you have a publicly owned railroad system which is in the process of recapitalizing its capital requirements that it uses out of its own earnings, that it borrows on the private market and that it obtains from the public through the Government of Canada, it has to be directed in an urgent priority manner into its transportation operations, the rehabilitation and updating of them. That means, aside from what will require financial capital assistance from the public on branch lines in the prairie provinces, that there needs to be a doubling of capital investment by Canadian National into its own plant that it considers to be commercially viable and profitable, excluding electrification.
Both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific have many hundreds of miles of railway lines that require hundreds of millions of dollars of investment. There is little purpose in recapitalizing Canadian National if all that is to be accomplished is to make Canadian National more like Canadian Pacific and then it is more profitable. If that is the objective, then I would be inclined to vote against this bill, which is why I said at second reading I could make just as good an argument against the legislation as I could for it. However, I am more of an optimist than I am a pessimist.
I worried about the motives of the government in terms of making Canadian National a private corporation. I received assurance from both the ministers and legal advice from the Department of Justice and others that there is no way they can sell off shares of Canadian National to the public without permission of parliament. Now I am worrying about the official opposition wanting to sell it off. The fact they do not want this bill to pass causes me to be suspicious about their motives regarding this legislation. When are we going to learn in this country that when you give priority to profits and profitability in a public utility, such as a transportation company, then the service that that public utility provides is going to suffer.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) talked about statutory rates, not only for grain and grain products but for livestock and livestock products. That is the only thing you can do in a country with as large a geography and as thinly and widely scattered population as we have. If not only your primary production, but your processing of raw products and manufacturing of products are going to occur in
5202

May 5, 1978
Railway Act
the prairies, the Atlantic region, northern Ontario or the Northwest Territories, then the nation as a whole must share the cost of moving the processed products and manufactured products to the markets of central Canada, the United States, and of other countries in the world.
The only way to share that cost is through statutory rates that apply to the processors and manufacturers of those products, and any deficit in the cost of moving those products is borne by the nationa as a whole. We have to move beyond just the Crow rates on grain. We have to move into livestock, livestock products, and the malting industry. In the Atlantic provinces we have to move into areas where they can process and manufacture because they know how to do it and are very good at it. These areas should not be discriminated against in transportation costs merely because of where they happen to live or be located.
If you have a transport policy and transport legislation that say profitability and competition shall be the criteria for your transportation costs, you will not be able to accomplish what I have suggested in terms of statutory rates. It would reverse the discrimination so that you would be discriminating in favour of, instead of against, areas of this nation and people who live in them. The nation as a whole shares the cost. It is called Confederation and such a policy would be a contribution to national unity.
Mr. Justice Emmett Hall and his commissioners were very wise in the recommendations they made regarding the extension of statutory freight rates to products other than grain and grain products. It is obvious that the principle should apply not only to the prairie provinces but to other outlying regions. It will be expensive, but why expect the industries and the populations of those regions to bear the cost by themselves? We could call it "co-operative federalism" or "renewed confederation," or whatever you like. We must share together if this country's unity is to mean anything at all.
Our nation has over one million people unemployed and yet there are several thousand miles of railway line that need rebuilding, 9,000 miles that should be electrified, plus we require approximately 25,000 to 30,000 new items of rolling stock. In the ten years I have been here it has come up every year-"not enough cars to haul potatoes out of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island-not enough stock cars". The hon. member for Medicine Hat ( Mr. Hargrave) will verify even better than I that that is the case. When I was a telegraph operator in 1948 there were not enough cars then, not enough locomotive power and not enough priority given by the government to rail passenger service. They are just playing around.
A good beginning for VIA Rail is ten sets of trains, but if you are not going to provide the finances and the policy backing, then it is doomed. In five years we will be writing it off as a dead loss unless it is given the kind of priority and opportunity that it deserves. Unless we reorganize transportation and quit the nonsense of flying multi-engine jet planes 200 or 300 miles when you can move passengers on the ground in a fast, efficient, comfortable, and reasonably priced system,

unless that kind of attitude and state of mind take place in transportation management of privately and publicly owned companies, in governmental policy and legislation, we are going to continue with this patchwork, hodge-podge transportation mess that the minister's predecessor baptized.
In making a move to recapitalize our national railway system that is publicly owned-the other one is not publicly owned but it was publicly paid for-and a move to do something about the financial mess and the bookkeeping of that company, it is nothing more than a first step. It is a beginning.
When things are done in my part of Canada that fly in the face of reason, equity, and the proper treatment of people and communities, such as the three recommendations of the so-called Prairie Rail Action Committee, and when primary producers have no opportunity to process their products or convey them to markets in central Canada and the United States because of geographical or climatic considerations, then we know that the difficulties of decades past will remain with us. Transportation is such an essential tool of economic development and national unity, such an essential part of the foundation of any national economy, that it requires a greater priority and capital investment than are envisaged by this government.
A year and one half ago when the government announced the $100 million program for branch line rehabilitation I was very pleased. I think only $30 million was spent on branch lines, however, and the other $70 million was spent on equipment for the railroads-which would have had to be purchased in any case. The minister used the figure of $600 million that I had used many years ago that would be required for that operation. Over the next six or seven years $1 billion per year will be needed if we are to do something about our transportation system. That is not inflationary. I am not going to worry about how much the financial critic of the official opposition or even the minister will cry about it. It just has to be done, and it is something that increases the assets of the nation, increases and strengthens our nationhood. It is not some sentimental desire to have choo-choo trains running around the country. It is an essential reordering of the way we communicate and move around the country. We cannot continue in the way we have been operating since 1881.
This is not some socialistic dogma, Mr. Speaker. It is a priority. We must use transportation in a better manner-as it is used in nation after nation around the world of all political stripes, from the extreme left to the extreme right. Only in Canada and in the United States do we cling to theories and principles that were out of date 40 years ago. Some of these principles and theories in transportation are hangovers from the railroad barons of the 1880's.
Subsequent to this legislation, which I hope passes next week, this government and the next government, and the two or three after that, must give priority to transportation and come up with a provision for the directing of capital investment. When this nation allows the Canadian Pacific Railway
May 5, 1978

to use its capital resources to buy something called the Syracuse China Corporation in Syracuse, New York, that is a disgrace. I think it is time for parliament and the government to tell the CPR that it is not going to buy the Syracuse China Corporation but that it is going to fix up its transportation equipment, invest in improved rail lines, faster trains, and electrification.
We cannot allow the profit motive to take priority over the transportation needs of the country as a whole. We direct that investment, and those who invest should receive a reasonable return and should have reasonable security. That is not too much to guarantee. Surely the government should have some say about that investment. If it means that the shareholders of the CPR have to take 50 cents or $ 1 less per share for a while, that could be regarded as their contribution along with the rest of the country to the rebuilding and enlarging of a transportation system to serve the people.
I regret that the official opposition has proposed a six-month on this legislation. I think the legislation does not go far enough, but we in this party approve of it as far as it goes so we will vote against the motion for a six-month hoist. While we will agree to passage of the legislation, I hope the government will use some imagination in the direction and the amount of funding available for our transportation systems. We could proceed more sensibly and begin now on such projects as rail line rehabilitation, electrification, faster intercity trains and other such improvements.
Another area where we must use better sense is the environment, and energy consumption. The research of energy consumption experts shows that an investment of $3 billion in Syncrude will be required and that one third of that amount invested in the electrification of 5,000 miles of railway track would save the same amount of crude oil as will be produced by Syncrude. Sufficient crude oil would be saved to enable farmers in the three prairie provinces to seed their crops, summer fallow their fields, and harvest their crops.
What are we waiting for, Mr. Speaker? There are one million people out of work and yet we are indulging in financial nit-picking on this bill. Let us get it out of the way. We will not object to passage of the legislation, and indeed will insist upon a lot more from whichever government is in power in order to rebuild and enlarge our transportation system on a scale that has not been seen since the CPR was built, and in a manner that will put an end to discrimination in transportation and which will ensure Confederation and national unity much more than in the past.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have noted that bills designed to make changes in the transportation system give rise to many comments, and that this is the case, of course, of the bill now under consideration since it concerns the transfer of a relatively large amount of money. Such a debate calls for many interventions. When we consider bill C-17, to amend Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act and to amend and repeal certain of the
Railway Act
statutes in consequence thereof, it is easy to see that it aims at solving a debt problem.
We often have the opportunity to discuss debt problems in today's topsy-turvy system. This is an area where Canadian legislators acquire some experience, since the administration is always faced with all types of debt problems. In March 1977, a way was found to convert the $842 million Seaway debt by providing a $625 million loan in shares held by the federal government for investment purposes and by converting $217 million into a loan which will gradually be cancelled by the 1 per cent profit that the Seaway will have to earn every fiscal year.
We have suggested at various times capital works financing methods by the Bank of Canada by means of which appropriate improvements could be made without getting the Canadian people constantly in debt. Unfortunately, the government does not find this procedure appropriate and prefers to remain deep in debt about which very few government members can say when it will be paid off. In the explanatory notes contained in Bill C-17, we find the following about clause 1:
These amendments would provide for a revision of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.
The new section 6 allows the governor in council to cancel, and I quote:
-not more than eight hundred and eight million dollars of the debt owed by the National Company to Her Majesty in right of Canada;
This includes the interest due after December 31, 1977. This section also provides for the consolidation of the remaining debts owed by the company to the Crown. Section 7 provides that the minister shall surrender to the company for cancellation all shares of the 4 per cent preferred stock of the company held by him on December 31, 1977. Section 8 provides for a new evaluation in the accounts of the company of its capital stock of no par value. Section 9 establishes the authorized and issued capital stock of the Canadian National at 6 million common shares of no par value and provides the value of these shares to be registered in the accounts of the company.
Under the amendments in clause 10, the company must pay to the Receiver General of Canada a dividend equal to 20 per cent of its annual earnings or to such higher percentage as determined by the governor in council. If we consider the terms of implementation of that financial amendment, we realize that a rather flexible accounting system should be established to adjust the expected variations, which shows that everything is controlled by money and that as usual Canadians will again have to pay high interest under that new debt readjustment plan. It is quite obvious that the difficulty in balancing a budget arises from accumulated debts and astronomical interest.
In 1972, the Canadian National long term debt was evaluated at $1,894 million. Interest paid over the last 25 years
80038-39(4

May 5, 1978
Railway Act
amounted to $1,334 million. As concerns the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority in 1972, its long term debt was $845 million. Interest paid since 1954 totals $141 million and, unpaid interest reaches $122 million. We realize that they were not even able to pay that interest and it is shocking that that kind of administration and our politicians continue to splash and flounder in an utterly confused system; they have been looking for a solution for many years without any success and they are facing complex problems. This is probably why the government chose to convert the St. Lawrence Seaway debt, as I said earlier.
Important changes should be made to the rail service. I already mentioned in this House that for various reasons railways have a social role to play. First a well organized passenger service is the safest and most comfortable transportation means, but as I said it should be well organized, which means convenient schedules, enough work crews to ensure the maintenance of the lines to avoid accidents, and comfortable cars, not only from Montreal to Toronto, but for people of every area of the country. Everybody appreciates comfort.
I have had the opportunity to experience the conditions in which rail service operates between Montreal and Toronto, and between Montreal and the Gaspe area. These conditions are not the same, and the lack of comfort inside individual cars is not the same either; why not maintain a passenger service which is universally satisfactory, no matter the region, instead of discriminating among the regions?
Hon. members are certainly aware that the Transport Act which the House adopted in 1960 set up the Canadian Transport Commission, with Mr. Pickersgill as its first President. He had created a position he could fill after retiring from Parliament. It is under his administration that the railways were allowed to abandon a number of passenger service runs, while others were maintained with government subsidies. I understand that people must be allowed to travel as they please either by train, by bus, or by plane, but we must also take the energy problem into account. We hear quite often about energy shortage. I sincerely think that by using the best incentives to encourage people to travel by train, we could make this type of transportation more financially rewarding and possibly also reduce the amounts of subsidies.
Railways in Europe and Asia are still very popular thanks to the improvement made in passenger services. One has to take into account the continuous increase in the cost of gasoline. Today you pay as much tax on a gallon of gas as the gas itself is worth. That is a factor which cannot be ignored and which would tend to increase the preference for a means of transportation which is as cheap as possible. The issue of the day is not whether we need to have the choice of a passenger transportation railway service but rather whether we must start preparing right now for the needs of future transportation by improv-
[Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).l
ing existing facilities and railway equipment. If we do not start working towards that now, within 10 years we will have to bear the enormous cost of starting anew. This is a decision which must be taken right now.
The issue is no longer whether Canadians prefer driving their cars instead of riding trains, whether businessmen whose travel expenses are generally paid for prefer the comfort of a jet plane to that of a train. Truck and bus services should complement rail services but not replace them. Even for long distance trips, high speed trains are the most pleasant means of transportation. Modern trains could offer restaurant cars, movies and television. You can take a stroll on a train and have a drink with new acquaintances while looking at the landscape instead of the clouds.
Furthermore, with a greater number of passengers, fares should stop increasing. Besides, it would be quite interesting to know how many millions or billions of dollars are spent on the construction and especially the maintenance of freeways and highways. Snow removal, patch paving in the spring, salt and calcium spraying, accident tolls, all these may not be included in the cost of a bus fare but they are actually paid for through income tax. The maintenance of a rail line is ten times cheaper. It is false to say that the public prefers the road network. It is rather the poor service presently offered by a railway system which has not evolved since 1920 which is responsible for it and has compelled people to turn towards the road network.
At first, considerable investments would be required. Stations would have to be made attractive, heated in winter, equipped with stores, restaurants, free parking lots for cars and bikes. It would be healthy for many people to get there by foot; for others, a local bus service would have to be provided. Where would we get the money? Just go around Montreal and look at the mass of asphalt on the roads-I could have named other cities-bridges, overpasses and tunnel crossings, and they cannot seem to be able to find the necessary funds to eliminate railway crossings that kill every year.
The important thing is to improve the train service. This would require the introduction of ultra-rapid trains, the elimination of railway crossings and even the fencing of the track. Today track maintenance is being delayed, and I had an opportunity to talk about this very often. Fences are being neglected, and farmers near railway tracks are always concerned, wondering whether they will be able to keep their cattle on their land or if they will slip through the CN fences. But those investments could become viable with time. The main improvements would be in the quality of life, the ecology and passenger comfort. This reorganization would undoubtedly result in lay-offs but a lot less than in the implementation of the plans now being considered. It would be a matter of giving employees the opportunity of being rehired by the reorganized railway companies.
May 5, 1978

At present, the more we study the federal government transport policy the more confused it looks; its various organizations are working at cross purposes undertaking contradictory projects that have nothing in common except that they all cost the taxpayers millions of dollars. The Canadian Railway Labour Association mentioned in the brief it submitted to the Government of Canada on March 20, 1978, that it still believed strongly that the National Transportation Act and or the Railway Act should be amended so as to include provisions dealing with the protection of employees affected by the changes the government made to Canadian railways in the public interest and by the amalgamation of present railway companies with larger public or private corporations.
I shall quote, from a brief, an excerpt which I consider timely:
In past briefs and, in particular, in those recently presented to the government, the Canadian Railway Labour Association asked that railway employees unions be consulted, and that the government take steps to protect employees when it makes changes in the railway transportation system in Canada.
When we intervene in this regard, because many employees are worried about the future of their jobs, we are always told sweetly: We will protect those employees and transfer them to other services. But the fact remains that Canadian National or Canadian Pacific employees still worry in the face of coming changes. To go back to my quotation:
We are happy to point out the fact that the government has accepted that principle...
It has accepted the principle; it is now a matter of working towards achieving that goal.
... principle for changes it made in passenger services in Canada. Meaningful consultations were held with the government in 1977. One of the results of the consultations with the Minister of Transport and the officials of the Department of Labour and the Department of Transport was order in council P.C. 19772987, which was passed on October 20, 1977.
We congratulate the government on that initiative and we see in the provisions on the regulations dealing with the assistance to be given railway companies and employees who have to adjust to the changes in the railway passenger services a progressive step which should underlie all alterations made in the railway system in Canada, no matter what government brings them in, for the protection of the employees affected by those changes.
Special attention must be given the matter of employees transfers, bearing in mind their seniority in the service. I travel quite frequently by train. I meet a lot of employees who have 30, 32 or 35 years' seniority and who are really concerned about what may happen to them. Last night, I listened to those who, in this House, spoke intelligently about pensions. I know many railway employees who are deeply concerned about the poor allottment of pensions. As for those who feel still capable of working, they have given several years of their lives to maintening the transportation system.
Of course a great many factors cannot be ignored in the reorganization of those services. Members of the United Transportation Union (conductors and brakemen), local 415 Charny and 721 Quebec, and of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, local 558, Quebec and Charny, have brought to the attention of the minister the possible disadvantages of the proposed changes. They produced evidence based on statistics they had to indicate that some of these changes, particularly
Railway Act
those related to the run along the CP tracks via Trois-Rivieres, will be much less popular and profitable than the present CN route via Ste. Foy and Drummondville. I have here the text of a rather recent editorial dated February 27, 1978, of CJRP radio station which clearly indicates that some of the proposed changes are far from improving the services. And I think it will be useful to quote the text of this editorial prepared by people well aware of the situation. It is entitled: Where are our railway services going?, and I quote:
We have seldom dealt with the problem of local railway services in our editorials. The population probably thinks that the removal of railway tracks in St. Roch puts an end to the problem. The Gare du Palais was replaced by some kind of waiting room near St. Sacrement Avenue and the Ste. Foy station was renovated, but now we learn that it will be closed soon.
Of course, I heard many comments on this subject during my trips. The Gare du Palais will probably be reorganized because they will finally understand that this station in downtown Quebec City should be readily accessible to travellers. That is what it was designed for in the first place. The changes made do not satisfy the public. The quotation goes further:
The "Via Rail" service will soon be introduced between Quebec City and Montreal. It will use the Canadian Pacific tracks on the north shore, thereby condemning to oblivion the Ste. Foy station which is very frequently used by the CN rapido trains.
We find a little abnormal that only one station, badly located at that, should serve the localities of the north shore. It seems unthinkable to us that no plan has been devised to provide Quebec City with better installations. Services should originate from a more central point, say Limoilou, at the rear of the Colisee, in order to connect Montreal through Ste. Foy. As a matter of fact, it has been noted recently that the viaducts needed for the CN lines already exist: on Highway 2, at Saules, on Highway 175 towards Chicoutimi, on First Avenue, on 22nd street and on La Canardiere. Consequently, the automobile traffic will not suffer. There is also another alternative, that is to use the maritime station of Foulons, which is already connected to the Ste. Foy station. Before, Quebec and Ste. Foy were well served by two stations, but soon there will be only one, and at a bad location.
Decisions such as those will not help the public see the advantages of train transportation. Moreover, millions are invested to upgrade the north shore lines, namely the CP line, while there is a sufficient number of good lines on the south shore. Besides, it should not be forgotten that it is the people of Ste. Foy who somehow filled the Rapidos. Perhaps that should be considered, instead of improving service by reducing it, in the hope that customers will also possibly decrease, which would be a pretext to discontinue the service altogether. That is a well known strategy of some North American carriers. Perhaps we should not consider Quebecers so dumb.
So, that is clear. I have had the opportunity to discuss it and we observe it regularly. Management tries to cut the staff down allegedly because that spells savings. Maintenance crews look after sections that are so long that they have a hard time doing their job, yet the number of office employees increases. Three or four $10,000 a year employees will be laid off so the company can put another $40,000 a year man behind a desk. That is definitely not the way to run a railroad, but it has been going on for a long time. The schedules are made up by those office people who know almost nothing of what a passenger service should be. I am certain of what I am saying; most of those who draw up the train schedules travel by car or plane. If they travelled more by train they would know what a well planned train schedule is.
Also, there is another thing those divisional office big shots forget, that is to consult the conductors and the train

May 5, 1978
Railway Act
employees. Some of them have 25, 30, 35 years of service and invaluable experience. Instead of consulting these people, our high salaried office big shots decide with pencils and maps where and when the train will stop.
That is the kind of decisions they take, with the result that people have deserted the train. People have tried other means of transportation, and this has created such deficits that the railways can no longer pay the interests and the government has to take over and assume the debt, which is exactly what they are doing. This morning I listened to the answer to a question put by my colleague about taxation, about tax transfer. For example, a new conception of the Social Credit Party of Canada was mentioned, that is not to give tax refunds directly to the citizens. I should say that when it comes to taxes, the government should try to reduce theirs. They have so many taxes in their own jurisdiction that they have no need to rummage in the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I have here a copy of the newspaper Le Devoir. It says it cost $ 100,000 a day to support the dollar. Is that the new idea of the government on how to maintain an adequate financial system? This is a strange conception, and I wonder where this is leading us. It is surely not the way to establish a just society and to distribute fairly among Canadians the opportunities to improve living conditions.
I will add in conclusion that it must be admitted that the rail service has not always received the necessary promotion. This is due to different factors, such as the schedule which I mentioned a while ago and which is often altered without any consideration for regional needs. As I said the officials of the CN passenger service should consult experts to establish their schedules. The conductors who have been travelling on the railroad for years are knowledgeable. They are acquainted with the problems. They have generally a well-disposed crew. I do not criticize the train service as such. The crew is generally well trained. They are nice people but they are under a team of individuals who know nothing about the needs of prospective passengers. I hope that those matters will be seriously studied and that effective decisions will be taken to improve appreciably passenger services in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, first I would draw attention to a couple of the remarks I made in this House during an earlier stage of this debate. As reported at page 4860 on April 25 I said:
The government has chosen to buy many rail cars for the west. I do not quarrel with that, if that is the right approach, but why has there not been a rationalized program to examine equipment shortages which exist across Canada and not just in the area of Canada in which the minister lives?
I would draw attention to one phrase I used in that quotation-the words "I do not quarrel with that".
[Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).l
As reported later, I said: "I do not want to be misinterpreted by any member of this House." I would almost think the minister qualifies in that category. I went on to say:
I do not begrudge the St. Lawrence Valley the policy that the Government of Canada is exercising, but I want the same policy in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
I said I have no quarrel with the ports policy being exercised in the St. Lawrence Valley.
Now I should like to quote from the minister, as reported at page 5053. The minister stated:
I find it extraordinary that a member of the Conservative Party can say that, when a colleague of his, a Conservative from New Brunswick, said in the debate the other day that we in this government are doing everything in transportation for the west.
Mr. Speaker, there is a sharp distinction of meaning between what I said and what the minister said, and he has pictured me in a mood which I did not express. I take umbrage at his accusation.

speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member has chosen to make that accusation against me I would ask him whether he would not also like on the record at the same time the words he used, as recorded at page 4860 of Hansard:
The government is selecting its political plums and spending its money in an unjust fashion, which brings about disunity in this nation. That is discrimination of the rankest kind. We are talking about the CNR and its recapitalization. We are going to double track through the Rockies, fix tracks across the prairies and examine tracks from Quebec City to Windsor-
That sounds to me like an accusation, a suggestion we are being unfair.

speechtext: Order, please. I think we are actually getting into a debate. The minister is allowed to correct a declaration made by the hon. member but not to make another one. Otherwise, we would have a debate between two members.
